answers: My boss said I had to finish by Friday.

what: A second correct form that the key marks wrong
reader: For every typed gap and every bank, try each other tense in the sentence. c-3118: She ___ in Madrid very long, but she knew the city well. (not / live): 'didn't live' is correct too. Fix with a situation (When I first met her … already), not by widening the key when the task is about one form.

what: Correct English marked wrong by a word bank
reader: Coffee ___ in Brazil (grows is correct), Two windows ___ in the storm (broke is correct), Mr Ozols asked whether the invoices ___ ___ sent (have been is correct). Read the sentence with every chip and every pair of chips.

what: An open gap that several words fit
reader: ___ you help me? takes can / could / will / would; There was ___ much traffic takes too / so. Use a choice with one fitting option, or accept every word.

what: The question and the answer are about different people
reader: ppc-B11-5a: 'Your friend is out of breath … Which sentence explains why?' with the answer 'I've been running.' Check who speaks in the answer.

what: Two matching pairs whose meanings can be swapped
reader: has been repaired = the work is finished / was repaired = it happened in the past; a plan / an arrangement. Swap any two right-hand sides: if both versions make sense, rewrite.

what: Two sentences joined with a comma in the task text
reader: fu-B11-5a: 'I will meet Anna at 6, we agreed yesterday.' The task text itself must be correct English.

what: A wrong option that nobody would choose, or that is correct English
reader: I meet Anna at 6 yesterday; The agent said I mighted need a visa. And the opposite: will freeze after 'If water gets very cold, it ___'. Each wrong option is a real form that a learner might choose and that is wrong in this sentence.

what: A report that is not a mistake
reader: c-0409: 'I was doing the shopping' was reported as wrong; do the shopping is correct (Murphy). Do not change correct English because of a report: check first.

what: The level label does not fit the sentence
reader: C1.1: We couldn't decide where ___ on holiday. (go). Compare the grammar and the words with docs/LEVEL-LISTS-test-english.md before giving a level.

what: A rewording that loses who is spoken to
reader: 'Report this request. Start with She: Please close the window.' Without 'to me', She asked him / us to close the window is as right as She asked me. When a tag is removed, check that the speaker AND the person spoken to are still known.

what: The moment of speaking is not fixed
reader: fu-B11-5a draft: 'A colleague asks about your evening.' Asked the next morning, I met Anna at 6 is the right answer. Say when (At lunch … your plans for this evening).

what: A reported statement that is still true
reader: 'I don't like coffee.' → Mark said he ___ coffee: doesn't like is correct too while it is still true. Give a situation that ends it (Ten years ago … Now he drinks it every day) or accept it with a note.

what: Generated word orders in a key that are not natural English or change the meaning
reader: If I liked jazz, he asked me. / The next day they said they would finish the report. Read every accepted answer of a typed task aloud; a start (Start with He asked me) must fit every accepted answer.

what: A task that can be solved without the grammar it is about (teacher, 11 November)
reader: Ask of every task: what does the learner have to know to get it right? 'I've been to Italy twice. = I have visited it two times in my life.' is matched by the word two. A choice whose three wrong options are in another time (I've met / I was meeting / I met for a plan this evening) is solved without knowing the future forms: the wrong options must compete (I'm meeting / I'll meet / I meet). A long situation in front of an easy choice is the same fault.

what: An instruction the learner may not understand
reader: 'Report it. Start with He asked me.' Learners may not know report. Show the quote and the start of the answer and let them complete it: 'Do you like jazz?' → He asked me ___.

what: An accepted word order that nobody says
reader: before it gets dark should we leave (generated). Read every accepted alternative aloud.

what: A typed conditional with both parts open and no situation
reader: If I ___ harder, I ___ the test. (study / pass): studied / would pass is as correct as had studied / would have passed. One situation sentence decides (I failed the test last week.).

what: A joining task that is only copying
reader: Join with if: You leave now. You will catch the train. At B1 the learner must change something (Leave now or you'll miss the train → If you don't leave now, …).

what: c-0737: If I ___ harder, I ___ the test. (study / pass): only had studied / would have passed accepted, but studied / would pass is correct too (report of 11 November)

task.q: If I ___ harder, I ___ the test. (study / pass)

what: The same mistake with the result first: I ___ her if I ___ her address. (visit / know) (11 November)

task.q: I ___ her if I ___ her address. (visit / know)

what: A situation sentence that leaves the first conditional possible (second reader, 12 November)
reader: 'Our company has fixed hours. If the company ___ more flexible hours, people ___ happier.' A fact that can still change allows offers / will be. The situation must make the condition unreal (will never change) or past.

what: The instruction names the answer (second reader, 12 November)
reader: 'Which sentence reports Sam's refusal' when the answer is 'Sam refused to…'; 'the customer's complaint' → 'complained'. Say 'answer', 'words'.

what: Matching by topic words instead of grammar (second reader, 12 November)
reader: 'I've been to Italy twice. = I can tell you what Rome is like.' Italy → Rome. Give all left sides the same topic so only the form decides ('I used to drink coffee / I'm used to drinking coffee / …'), or do not use matching for it.

what: A one-key typo in a word copied from the task marked a correct sentence wrong (report of 12 November)
reader: 'wheh I finish the report, I'll call you.' The grader now accepts a neighbouring-key slip in a copied word (not in a last letter that can be an ending); tested in correct_part_test.php.

what: The instruction contains the answer (report of 12 November)
reader: 'Complete with will have to: Tomorrow we ___ leave early.' The learner copies the words. Give the verb in brackets and a situation (Our train is at 5 a.m., so tomorrow we ___ leave very early. (have to)).

what: An open gap with nothing that points to the answer (report of 12 November)
reader: 'Children ___ to enter without an adult.' (aren't allowed): want, need, have, are not able all fit or nearly fit. Give the situation (The sign says…) and a word bank with real forms that do not fit.

what: A word order whose cards make another correct sentence when who asks whom is not given (report of 13 November)
reader: 'she asked if I could help her': the same cards give 'I asked her if she could help'. Say who speaks to whom before the task (Anna's question to you: 'Can you help me?').

what: A long situation before an easy choice (report of 13 November)
reader: 'You want to say your report was finished in March. Choose the correct option.' Say only Choose the correct option, and put the time word in the sentence (I ___ my report last March). A situation only where the form depends on it, and then as natural as possible.

what: A typed question whose key drops words the learner may keep (report of 13 November)
reader: 'Make a question with What: You are going to cook dinner.' → What are you going to cook for dinner? is correct too. For every Make a question task, also accept the question that keeps the rest of the sentence or leaves out an extra phrase (Why did he leave?).

what: A long situation before an easy choice (report of 13 November)

task.q: You want to say your report was finished in March, and you are telling your manager about it now. Choose the correct option.
wrong: I have finished it in March.

what: A word order where an article card can move to another noun (report of 14 November)
reader: 'if you add salt the soup tastes better': the cards also give 'if you add the salt, soup tastes better', which is correct. Move every the / a card to each other noun and read the sentence; accept what is correct or change the sentence.

what: A new task without a grammar point (14 November, C1): the app could not choose the next task from the same point

task.q: I ___ never ___ to Japan. (be)

what: An advice task without a problem to advise on (report of 14 November, c-0707)
reader: 'Give advice with If I were you: Tell your boss.' read as an order with no problem to advise on (a learner advised 'increase my salary'); 'Give advice with If I were you and buy a new laptop' then gave the whole answer away. An advice task gives the problem in one sentence and lets the learner write the form: Your friend's laptop is old and very slow. If I ___ you, I ___ a new one. (be / buy). Avoid your / my after If I were you and advice about talking to someone (teacher, 14 November).

what: ia-C12-5a: a wrong option that scrambles the article instead of showing a mistake of the point (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: 'How funds were the spent remains to be investigated' tests nothing about question clauses. Every wrong option is a believable mistake of the point: question word order (How were the funds spent remains…), an extra it, a plural verb after the clause (…remain to be investigated).

what: ia-C11-6a: a writing check whose feedback did not name the learner's real mistake (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: 'the questions is how to have balance' got only 'Start with The question is + a question word'. Write each must so that one message names one mistake (questions is → question is; how can we → how we can), and test the checks with the learners' own sentences.

what: psp-A22-5a: a wrong option nobody would choose in a meaning question (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: 'Why do we say Tickets are sold here?' had 'The tickets are very old and cheap.' A wrong option in a meaning question is a believable misunderstanding of the form (sold read as the past; are sold read as someone is selling now).

what: Which sentence has a mistake? with a mistake nobody makes, and three copies of it as the right sentences (tester's report, 21 November: rv-C12-4a, c-2089, c-3426, c-1693)
reader: He recommended to reading…, I will to meet you…, we would are in Rome…, You needn't to come early next to You needn't come early: the copies give the pair away and the mistake is too obvious. Use a mistake learners make (She suggested me to book…, I call you as soon as I land, If we would have caught the flight…) and three correct sentences about three other things. Not recommend + me + to: that pattern is accepted in British English.

what: cs-B12-2a: a matching task with one pair from another context (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: Three car sentences and 'If you heat ice, it melts. = This is always true.' The odd one is matched by its topic, not its form. Keep one context in all four pairs and make every label fit only one sentence (I have no car / I had no car then / This is what usually happens / It is possible in the future).

what: c-0182: a matching task that needs general knowledge and has two swappable pairs (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: 'Match each famous thing with who made it' (Hamlet / Harry Potter = was written by…): the learner needs literature, not grammar, and the two was written by endings swap. Only the grammar may decide: a short answer with its own pronoun for each question (Were the photos taken in Rome? = No, they weren't.).

what: Word orders whose second correct order was refused (tester's report and learners' data, 21 November: c-1824, c-1822, c-1393, c-2233)
reader: my parents read a newspaper every day but they never watch the news (clauses swapped with the subject first); I usually don't drink coffee… (usually before don't is correct); could you please pass me the salt; that jacket is cheaper than this one (this / that swapped). Try every clause order, every adverb position, please in each place and every swap of this / that, the / a and the people; also remove generated orders that are not English (please you could pass me the salt).

what: c-2206: a task whose answer is the example on its point card (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: Correct the mistake: We had been knowing each other since school, while the card's mistake line and watch line show We'd known each other for years. Three tasks of the point used know each other. Compare every task of a point with its card (examples, mistakes, watch lines) and use another sentence.

what: c-3182, c-3185: a choice with only two wrong options where the common learner mistake was missing (teacher, 21 November)
reader: We ___ to Spain last summer (goed / gone) and She ___ her keys two days ago (losed / has lost): add the mistake Latvian learners make, be + base or be + past form (were go, was lost), and check that it is wrong in the sentence.

what: c-2948: a present perfect for an action that is finished (teacher, 21 November)
reader: I've charged it all night, but my phone still won't switch on: the charging is over, so I charged it all night. Read the tense of every sentence that frames the tested form, not only the gap.

what: c-2361: a correct word refused in a one-word gap (tester's report, 21 November)
reader: It was a difficult task, and ___ they finished it on time accepted yet | still and refused nevertheless. For every one-word gap list every word that is correct there (nevertheless, nonetheless), with a note when one is more formal.

what: rs-B21-3a: a report with told me to refused (learners' data, 21 November)
reader: 'You must finish by Friday.' → My boss told me ___. accepted only that-clauses; to finish by Friday is the usual report of an order. In report gaps after told me, try both told me to + verb and told me (that) + clause.

what: c-2243: a rewrite whose instruction let learners reverse the meaning (learners' data, 21 November)
reader: Rewrite with less ... than: This flat is more expensive than that flat. Six learners wrote This flat is less expensive than that flat. Give the start that keeps the meaning (Start with That flat), never the answer.

what: Indirect questions: the direct question is quoted and the frame is given, so only two words change places (teacher, 21 November: 'too easy')
reader: 'Where is the toilet?' Could you tell me where ___ ___? (the toilet / is). The learner copies the words and swaps two. Give a situation or a frame whose gap holds the subject AND the verb (Do you know where ___ the car last night? (Tom / park) → Tom parked), a sentence to correct, or a need to ask about (gp6_iq_b1.py). Tasks of this kind stay only as practice.

what: A writing task whose instruction already says the indirect question (teacher's tester, 21 November: ip-B11-6a, ip-B12-6a)
reader: 'Ask a colleague politely where the meeting room is. Start with Could you tell me.' The instruction gives 'where the meeting room is' in statement order: the learner only adds the start. Give the situation (you have just joined a gym and can't find the pool) and let the learner build the question.

what: Which sentence has a mistake? with the correct twin of the wrong sentence among the options (tester, 21 November: ip-B12-4a, ip-B11-4a, c-0914)
reader: I wonder what does she want. / I wonder what she wants. / … The pair gives the answer away. The three correct sentences are about three different things, with other frames and tenses (Do you know whether the museum has reopened? / I wonder who will win the match tonight. / I'm not sure how much we paid for the hotel.).

what: A politeness choice whose wrong options are rude sentences (tester, 21 November: ip-B11-5a 'the wrong sentences are not good samples')
reader: 'Choose the most polite option' with 'You, where is the nearest post office?' and 'Tell me where …, please.' is solved without the grammar. The wrong options must be the real mistakes of the point (does it take / it take / takes it).

what: A typed polite question that accepts only one wording (tester, 21 November: c-3413 'Do you know when the shop closes?' refused 'what time the shop closes')
reader: When the learner builds the question, every question word that asks the same thing is correct (when / what time; Do you happen to know …). List them; for an open need (Ask about the shop), list every core answer or use a write task with checks.

what: Indirect-question choices whose wrong options miss the real mistake (21 November: c-0912, c-0894, c-0898, as ip-B12-1a on 27 October)
reader: Could you tell me ___ the library is open? if / that / what / did. Nobody writes 'that' or 'what' here; the real mistake is leaving out if (Could you tell me is the library open?). Give the real mistakes as options: if there are / are there / if are there / there are.

task.model: Could you tell me where the meeting room is?
